title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 1.1**
Oṃ. Homage to glorious Vajrasattva (the Adamantine Being, the primordial buddha of this tradition).
**CMP 1.2**
Pay homage to the One pure as space and without inherent nature; pay homage to the Whole that is syllable-less and beyond utterance. Pay homage to the all-pervading Sugata who has not [yet] come; pay homage to the One who is wholly, entirely, and in every respect empty.
**CMP 1.3**
"One should rely upon the meaning (arthapratiśaraṇa (reliance on the import rather than the letter)); as for the word, [let it be] however it may." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 1.4**
In the tantra: "Of the eighty-four thousand dharma-aggregates of the Great Sage, those who do not know the [single] reality [contained in them]—they are all [striving] in vain." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 1.5**
Therefore he says: "As a joining-together for the ādikarmika (beginner in practice) in the descent into ultimate [reality], skillful means too has been fashioned by the perfectly awakened ones, like a staircase." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 1.colophon**
[Here ends] the first chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration (melāpaka (blending, coalescence of the tantric stages)) of awakening. // 1 //
**CMP 2.1**
In brief, the five aggregates (skandha (the five constituents of the person)) are proclaimed to be the five Buddhas; the adamantine sense-fields (āyatana (sense-bases)) themselves are the foremost maṇḍala (ritual circle, divine palace) of the bodhisattvas.
**CMP 2.2**
Earth is declared to be Locanā; the water-element is remembered as Māmakī; fire would be the one named Pāṇḍarā; wind is proclaimed [the consort] Tārā.
**CMP 2.3**
By means of form, sound, and the rest, the mantra-practitioner should always meditatively cultivate (bhāvanā (meditative cultivation, realization)) the deity.
**CMP 2.4**
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the glorious Guhyasamāja (the Secret Assembly tantra, root tantra of this tradition) Great Yoga Tantra.
**CMP 2.5**
The [buddha-]families are taught to be of a hundred kinds, but in brief fivefold; and again they become threefold through the division into body, speech, and mind.
**CMP 2.6**
"In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed to be the five Buddhas."
**CMP 2.7**
Resting on the five hearts [of the buddha-families], issued from the five [subtle] bodies, conjoined with the five winds, [the body] is made for the enjoyment of the five sense-pleasures. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.8**
Because it goes forth as the [out-]breathing (prāṇāyāma (breath/wind control)) and runs forth at all times through the sense-doors along their threads, it is called prāṇa (the forward-moving breath).
**CMP 2.9**
Because it carries away wind, urine, feces, and likewise semen and the rest, this is apāna (the down-voiding breath), as the yogins always observe.
**CMP 2.10**
That which constantly assimilates from every side what is eaten, chewed, licked, drunk, and sucked is called samāna (the digestive, equalizing breath).
**CMP 2.11**
By upward motion, by drawing together, and by the consuming of foods to be chewed and eaten, this [breath] is to be known as the action of udāna (the upward breath), through its union with cognition.
**CMP 2.12**
Pervading and sustaining, and going and coming and the like—because it pervades all the joints, it is called vyāna (the diffused breath).
**CMP 2.13**
Earth is declared to be Locanā; the water-element is remembered as Māmakī; fire is declared to be Pāṇḍarā; wind is proclaimed [as] Tārā.
**CMP 2.14**

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
Aggregate, element, and likewise sense-faculty—each fivefold, divided into five—each one of them is blessed and empowered by a Tathāgata: whence then could the deeds of saṃsāra arise [from them]?
**CMP 2.15**
Likewise the five external objects too, each one of them, are by the five Tathāgatas—each by its own—forever blessed; and the threefold knowledge rests upon the five.
**CMP 2.16**
One should contemplate the maṇḍala born of the all-adamantine, situated in the midst of the space-element, and should also perform the dissolution, if the bearer of the peaceful vajra so wishes. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.17**
The body of human beings is seen to be of fivefold nature, fixedly [composed] of just the five elements; cultivating their own mind, [also] fixed, by the existence and non-existence of those [elements], [practitioners] become Buddhas. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.18**
In the Khasama-tantra too he says (in Apabhraṃśa-flavored verse): "This whole world has the nature of the five Buddhas—behold the wondrous, variegated divine play! Therein indeed One, called Great Bliss, dances—One [yet] manifold—through the [varied] savor [of experience]." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.19**
"But in brief, fivefold."
**CMP 2.20**
Through the [meditative] settling of body, speech, and mind, [their] inherent nature is not apprehended; through the practice of the mantra-as-embodiment there is neither awakening nor [any reified] cultivation.
**CMP 2.21**
Having examined this in brief—the characteristic of body, speech, and mind—one should cultivate the concentration (samādhi (meditative absorption)) framed by mantra, conjoined with the [ritual] procedure. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.22**
[True] union does not arise in mere reflected images, in cast [icons] and the like; therefore, for the yogin of the great yoga of bodhicitta (awakening-mind; here also the subtle wind/seminal essence), the deities [are the practitioner's own reality].
**CMP 2.23**
The self is indeed the buddhahood of all the Buddhas, and the very heroic nature of the [awakening] being; therefore, through union with one's own tutelary deity, one should accomplish [realization in] the self alone. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 2.24**
With a body settled in mantra, with speech, and impelled in the mind, one should accomplish the supreme attainment (siddhi (spiritual accomplishment)), beloved as the contentment of the mind.
**CMP 2.colophon**
[Here ends] the second chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] the isolation of body (kāyaviveka (isolation of body, a completion-stage phase)). // 2 //
**CMP 3.1**
The great jewel of five colors, only about the size of a mustard seed, one should always cultivate with effort at the tip of the nose through yoga. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.2**
[Cultivate] the breath as consisting of the five knowledges and having the nature of the five elements.
**CMP 3.3**
Having let it issue forth, one should imagine the great jewel of five colors in condensed form at the tip of the lotus-nose; this is remembered as prāṇāyāma (breath-control).
**CMP 3.4**
Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, replied to the one who was expounding the meaning of the vajra-recitation, after the Teacher of the world had duly paid homage [to him].
**CMP 3.5**
This bodhicitta that has been revealed is only of mundane import (laukika (worldly, conventional)).
**CMP 3.6**
How then will those still to come [in the future] realize the transcendent (lokottara (supramundane, world-transcending)) [bodhicitta]?

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 3.7**
The Dharma was indeed taught by you for the abandonment of all [false] views; how then is bodhicitta [taught such that] that very view is firmly fixed [again]?
**CMP 3.8**
Bewildered by the intentional, twilight language (saṃdhyābhāṣā (intentional, coded twilight-language of tantra)), they do not understand the meaning that is spoken; they grasp it just as it sounds, and accordingly they [merely] cook [their own confusion / ripen ill results].
**CMP 3.9**
Then the all-pervading Blessed One would say to Vajrapāṇi: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Secrets! By you the [need of those] to come [in future] has been [well] explained."
**CMP 3.10**
Bodhicitta is the wind, abiding in space, the very life-breath of beings, fivefold in nature and bearing ten names.
**CMP 3.11**
It is called the twelve-membered [chain of] dependent [origination]; by [its own] nature it becomes threefold. This, foremost of all the faculties, is the bodhicitta termed "wind."
**CMP 3.12**
Unmanifest, it is thus [called] subtle; [manifest,] it is called manifest. Resting upon it, a person performs deeds and engages objects and the rest.
**CMP 3.13**
[The rites of] pacifying, increasing, and likewise subjugating and fierce [magic]—all that [proceeds] from bodhicitta, from [its] resting upon the abode of the three realities.
**CMP 3.14**
And however many varied conventional designations of "light" (āloka (the inner radiances/lights of the dissolution sequence)) are imagined, they arise from bodhicitta; the conceptual constructions always [arise] from the wind.
**CMP 3.15**
The phenomenon of pleasure, pain, and the rest is produced from the [same] seed alone; this has the nature of bodhicitta, comparable to the [primordial] non-duality of the aggregates and the rest.
**CMP 3.16**
Through the single union of wisdom and means (prajñopāya (the union of insight (prajñā) and method (upāya))), bodhicitta becomes [the whole] world.
**CMP 3.17**
The master should recite [it] by himself, free of [discursive] meditation and study.
**CMP 3.18**
By the division of day and night, through the conjunction of moon and sun, the out-breath, pervading the world, is the one wind that is bodhicitta.
**CMP 3.19**
Having abandoned the fruit, good and ill, it becomes indeed space-like. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.20**
[Knowing] those named prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna, and [the five lesser winds] Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
**CMP 3.21**
—having made this image of oneself and then having generated the reality of the consort. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.22**
[The recitation-syllables/cyclic permutations:] koṭākṣa, koṭava, koṭa, koṭābha, and koṭīraka; kolākṣa, kolāva, kola, kolābha, and likewise kali. [These are the cycled phonemes of the vajra-recitation.]
**CMP 3.23**
Arising from the aperture of the nose, abiding in the five buddha-families, the fivefold wind, moving upward, courses through the body without cease.
**CMP 3.24**
From its conventional coursing through the nostril, issuing out from that door, these are fourfold: [those of] the left, the right, the pair [of both together], and the still [or blocked].
**CMP 3.25**
From the right, the element flows forth as the maṇḍala of fire; this red-colored mouth [-aspect], of the Lotus Lord [Amitābha], courses [there].
**CMP 3.26**
And from the left, the element flows forth, issued from the maṇḍala of wind, green and dark-hued; that of the Action Lord [Amoghasiddhi] courses [there].
**CMP 3.27**
The flow of the pair is the element of golden color, [together] with its triple [aspect], and the maṇḍala of earth (Mahendra); that of the Jewel Lord [Ratnasambhava] courses [there].

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 3.28**
The still one [has] no outward flow; in a moment [it becomes] the water-maṇḍala (Vāruṇa); resembling pure crystal, that of the Vajra Lord [Akṣobhya] courses [there].
**CMP 3.29**
Having drawn up the whole element, held as both container and contained, the great body of Vairocana issues forth at the moment of death.
**CMP 3.30**
This [recitation of] the four maṇḍalas one should recite always, concentrated; the recitation of mantra-practitioners goes on continuously day and night, by the [proper] count of recitation.
**CMP 3.31**
He who, [counting] from one up through nine, is not bound by the ten—him one should know as unbound; he knows the supreme state.
**CMP 3.32**
The vowel- and consonant-phonemes, conforming to the number nine, in their unbound mutual combination—he who knows them is the Teacher of the world.
**CMP 3.33**
He who, having awakened, desires the attainment, the wealth of the fruit of liberation—he, formless, attains that very [goal] which is free of form.
**CMP 3.34**
Conjoined with the terminal element, abiding in the sixteen [phases] beginning with the first digit (kalā), joined with the set of five fives, and yoked with the three [or four]—
**CMP 3.35**
—with the nasal anusvāra and with the long [vowel], subject to the conjunction and elision of the grade-vowel (guṇa), the whole [recited] utterance would be short, neither manifold nor single.
**CMP 3.36**
By the meaning of the syllable ya, whatever is to be done is to be done by one who desires attainment; by the triad beginning with the r-sound (repha), the activity of the world proceeds.
**CMP 3.37**
The phonemes that are spoken from behind, and those again that face forward—these, [classed as] feminine, masculine, and neuter, are constructed [in correspondence] with the elements and the rest.
**CMP 3.38**
Joined below and above, known and applied with [discerning] intellect—what is taught by the six [is born] from the four, three, and one, [and is itself] born of the single existent that is without inherent nature.
**CMP 3.39**
Having yoked [the syllables] in the meaning of the first [triad] and the rest, the knowledge of the three times arises; like a dream or a magical illusion, having dispelled [the duality], one would [recognize/perform] the world within the triple realm.
**CMP 3.40**
This mantra is a withdrawal [of the senses] (pratyāhāra), born of a nature that is without inherent nature; the form transformed from it is what brings about the apprehension of the deity.
**CMP 3.41**
Conventional, abiding in the three realities, having the character of the recitation [arising from one's own] nature—this is the supreme bodhicitta, unnameable and unutterable.
**CMP 3.42**
That very [bodhicitta] would be the triad-as-one, without going forth and without coming, unceasing and wholly at peace, free of eternalism and annihilationism.
**CMP 3.43**
Its conceptual construction undone by the knower of the three times, having the character of non-difference from space—this indeed is the ultimate, having the character of being known each for oneself (pratyātmavedya (to be realized inwardly, each for oneself)).
**CMP 3.44**
In all activities indeed, in sitting and the rest, the knower of yoga should always recite [it]—the unnameable, the unutterable, [that which is] beyond the three times.
**CMP 3.45**
The recitations beginning with Pāṇḍarā are taught [to number] two hundred twenty-five; correctly multiplied by four, with the fourfold yoke, [they make] nine hundred.

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 3.46**
And the nine hundred that is observed, with [its] twenty-four circuits, becomes—through their re-arising—twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths per day].
**CMP 3.47**
Thus, in secret twilight-intention, the subtle yoga has been revealed; though free of [discursive] meditation and study, it is nonetheless called "recitation."
**CMP 3.48**
The syllable A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great import, the supreme imperishable; it is the great life-breath, the very non-arising, free of vocal articulation; it is the foremost cause of all expression, the radiant clear-light (prabhāsvara (clear light, luminosity)) of all speech. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.49**
[Cultivate] in the center of the heart the unstruck [sound], blazing like a lamp—the supreme, subtle imperishable, the syllable A, the supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.50**
These dharmas are designated through the sounding of words; yet neither dharma nor word is apprehended herein. And [only] by descending into the unity [of things], into [their true] dharma-nature, will one touch the unsurpassed, supreme acceptance (kṣānti). Thus [it is said].
**CMP 3.colophon**
[Here ends] the third chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] the isolation of speech (vāgviveka (isolation of speech, a completion-stage phase)). // 3 //
**CMP 4.1**
Those who [properly] settle the mind—far-going, lone-wandering, bodiless, lying hidden in the cave [of the heart]—are released from the bondage of Māra. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 4.2**
Whatever mind arises dependently through the sense-faculties and their objects—
**CMP 4.3**
—that "mind" (manas) is so called from the syllable sa, in the sense of "protecting" (trāṇana), [as it is renowned in the eighty(-thousand teachings)]. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 4.4**
Cognition is mere bare awareness (saṃvittimātra (mere bare cognition/awareness)), markless like space; yet it has a division, as twilight, night, and day [i.e. the three lights].
**CMP 4.5**
Radiance, radiant-glow, and likewise radiance-attainment—mind is thus said to be threefold (āloka-ālokābhāsa-ālokopalabdhi (the three inner radiances/lights of the dissolution sequence)); its support is [now] declared.
**CMP 4.6**
By the wind in its subtle form, cognition has reached a state of [intimate] mixture [with it].
**CMP 4.7**
Having issued out along the paths of the senses, it rests upon [its] objects.
**CMP 4.8**
When the wind, joined with the [inner] glow, has become the vehicle, then all that [stream of] mental factors (prakṛti) proceeds, scattered and in disarray.
**CMP 4.9**
Wherever the wind is stationed, it would carry forth that very mental factor. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 4.colophon**
[Here ends] the fourth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] the isolation of mind (cittaviveka (isolation of mind, a completion-stage phase)). // 4 //
**CMP 5.1**
Just as the manifold rain-clouds, of various shapes and colors, having arisen from the expanse of the sky, go to dissolution there [in that same sky]—
**CMP 5.2**
—so all the mental factors, caused by the three glows [the three lights], having entered into all their objects, [then] enter into the clear light (prabhāsvara (clear light, luminosity)).
**CMP 5.3**
Of such a nature, [proceeding] from consciousness [yet] veiled by the film of ignorance, having done good and ill deeds, [beings] wander in the five destinies.
**CMP 5.4**
Having done the deeds of immediate retribution and the rest, one ripens in the hells; having done the good deed of giving and the rest, one is exalted in the heavens and so forth.

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 5.5**
Having thus obtained, again and again, an endless thousand births, one grieves out of delusion, [thinking] "This is the ripening of former karma."
**CMP 5.6**
And those persons who are afflicted, [bound] by the procedure of the natural glow—having known this, the wise are freed from the cage of existence. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 5.7**
[Objection:] If all this is empty and of unarisen nature, how do karma, and pleasure and pain, operate here in saṃsāra?
**CMP 5.8**
[Reply:] By the [notions of] "I" and "mine" and likewise by the stains of passion and the rest, [the world] is constructed by the dependent [nature, paratantra]; through suffering the foolish are afflicted.
**CMP 5.9**
All this is mind-only (cittamātra (mind-only, cognition-only)), arisen like the work of a magician; from that [comes] good and ill karma, and from that [comes] good and ill birth. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 5.colophon**
[Here ends] the fifth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] the division of action (karman). // 5 //
**CMP 6.1**
Through the cultivation of reality one attains a body resembling the rainbow (indrāyudha (rainbow, lit. 'Indra's weapon'; the illusory/rainbow body of the adept)). Thus [it is said].
**CMP 6.2**
When, with regard to aggregate, element, sense-field, faculty, and the rest, the two cognitions abide there equally, then, this great emptiness being present, one who has fallen asleep would indeed behold a dream, by the force of the wind.
**CMP 6.3**
Between the dreaming and the waking [state] there is no other difference; the one desiring the fruit of the dream would [merely] imagine [one]. By day and night the dream comes upon the creature; in the density of [the element] earth it has slept for a very long time.
**CMP 6.4**
When the fruit of the deed done is not [yet] ripe, the wind moves on again into [a new] birth here; when the fruit has become ripe, the wind, having departed, [moves] elsewhere—for swift indeed is death in the world.
**CMP 6.5**
Just as the Lord of Conquerors, established in the ten directions—and there is no marrow, bone, or flesh in his body—would [yet] enter [a body] for the welfare of beings, and accomplishes his task by way of fashioning the [bodily] elements [as illusion]—
**CMP 6.6**
—so, in due order, one whose mind is [as if] asleep while waking would [merely] wish for a fruit, [which is] a web of conceptual constructions. All dharmas are indeed dream-like; they are neither false nor not-false, for there is the absence of both [alternatives]. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 6.colophon**
[Here ends] the sixth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya (conventional, relative truth)). // 6 //
**CMP 7.1**
Just as a lamp set within a pot does not shine forth outside, but once that pot is broken the lamp's flame thereupon shines forth—
**CMP 7.2**
—one's own body indeed is the pot; reality itself is the lamp; when [the pot] is broken by the mouth [-instruction] of the guru, buddha-knowledge becomes manifest.
**CMP 7.3**
He sees space [merge] with space arisen [from space], sky [merge] with sky; just so, this practice has been shown forth from the mouth of the guru. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 7.4**
These dharmas are designated through the sounding of words; yet neither dharma nor word is apprehended herein. And [only] by descending into the unity [of things], into [their] dharma-nature, will one touch the unsurpassed, supreme acceptance. Thus [it is said].

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 7.5**
Homage to you, boon-granting foremost Vajra; homage be to you, Limit of the Real (bhūtakoṭi)! Homage to you, Womb of Emptiness; homage be to you, Awakening of the Buddhas!
**CMP 7.6**
Grant me, O great master, the vision of full awakening, the great knowledge of all the Buddhas, the unsurpassed all-emptiness.
**CMP 7.7**
Grant me, O great being, [that which has] the sole character of self-experience, freed from karma and birth; may I attain awakening here in this very [life].
**CMP 7.8**
Apart from the lotus of your feet there is no other refuge, O Lord; therefore be gracious, foremost of Buddhas, Hero of the world, Great Sage!
**CMP 7.9**
Having thus praised [him] with that divine, supreme rite of supplication, the glorious guru, an ocean of virtues, gives rise to compassion for the disciple—
**CMP 7.10**
—becoming serene of countenance, compassionate, and gladdened, he should impart [to him] the divine supreme pledge (samaya (sacred pledge, commitment)) that springs from the yoga-tantra.
**CMP 7.11**
Then the master, concentrated, should bring forth bodhicitta, and having deposited the bodhicitta in a vase or a conch—
**CMP 7.12**
—then, having summoned that disciple, blessed and empowered by all the Buddhas, he should bestow on him the pledge, endowed with the seal (mudrā) of the Conqueror.
**CMP 7.13**
The consecration (abhiṣeka (consecration, empowerment)) is to be given by the second Vajra-holder [the vajra-master], with auspicious uttered words and with the varied sounds of [many] instruments.
**CMP 7.14**
By the consecration of the triple realm, the disciple, with bowed head and joined palms—then, being urged thereto, [the master] should give to him what is [thereby] authorized.
**CMP 7.15**
The garland, the water, the fully-awakened [crown], the vajra, the bell, then the mirror, the name, and the authorization of [becoming] a master—this indeed is the sequence of consecration.
**CMP 7.16**
Then he should bestow upon him the mark of the outer full awakening, that which has been received in the [lineage] tradition, come down through the succession of gurus. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 7.17**
The yogin should constantly recollect the drop (bindu) that dissolves into clear water, in a river or a lake—[that] pure [drop], explained step by step in [its] sequence of distinctions; just as in a mirror the gradual vanishing of the breath-mist comes about and is no longer perceived in that manner, so the sequence [of practice], [namely] the apprehension of the condensed [drop], is to be discerned thus by those who follow the [proper] procedure.
**CMP 7.18**
Beyond the cultivation of all the limbs [of practice], free of conceiving and the conceived, wholly transcending [even] the [smallest] measure and drop—this is the supreme maṇḍala.
**CMP 7.19**
He who enters the stainless [reality] of all existents, in [their] forms and formlessnesses—the mind, awakened and impelled, [is] the maṇḍala, having the form of the maṇḍala.
**CMP 7.20**
"It is" and "it is not"—both are extremes; "pure" and "impure"—these too are extremes. Therefore, abandoning both extremes, the wise one does not even take a stand in the middle. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 7.21**
In the sense of "endless as space," the great resting-place of all beings—[that is the] glory, the splendor, the radiant King, the fulfiller of all hopes.
**CMP 7.22**
Oh the Buddha! Oh the Buddha! Oh the teaching of the Dharma! O bodhicitta, whose meaning is the pure reality, whose import is pure—homage be to you!

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 7.colophon**
[Here ends] the seventh chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] ultimate truth (paramārthasatya (ultimate, absolute truth)). // 7 //
**CMP 8.1**
They call the coarse [level] that which consists of sound; the subtle, likewise, that which consists of mind; that which is devoid of mind is the supreme state of the yogins. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 8.2**
That reality is to be experienced for oneself; it cannot be told to another. It is to be reached through devotion and cultivation, and cannot be reached otherwise.
**CMP 8.3**
Having known reality, then having made devotion day and night—in that supreme nirvāṇa, the peaceful, unsurpassed state—
**CMP 8.4**
—then, by the power of that devotion, fashioned by the strength of cultivation, there arises in him a certain supreme form, born of bliss.
**CMP 8.5**
Arisen all at once ("dhag!") into manifest shape, blazing forth yet [also] taking the form of dissolution, illuminating all this—earth, atmosphere, and heaven—together with [all] moving and unmoving things.
**CMP 8.6**
By the force and power of cultivation, [it is] the blissful [state] consisting of wisdom and means, wholly freed from all afflictions, adorned with all [auspicious] marks.
**CMP 8.7**
Arisen from the knowledge of emptiness, free of duality, supremely blissful, endowed with the best of all aspects, free of grasped and grasper.
**CMP 8.8**
Cognition is illusion-like, pure, limpid, naturally stainless, transcending sound, smell, and taste, and likewise free of touch.
**CMP 8.9**
It is seen, supremely, only in samādhi, with the eye of knowledge—divine, like a shadow or an illusion, possessed of a divine form.
**CMP 8.10**
With its garland of surging waves of knowledge, [taking] manifold, various bodily forms—those who cultivate reality attain a body resembling the rainbow (indrāyudha (rainbow; the illusory rainbow-body of the adept)).
**CMP 8.11**
By the power of the yoga of cultivation and by the keeping of the pledges, such a form is attained—one that is not to be uttered even by the Conquerors.
**CMP 8.12**
Where there is no body, speech, or mind—the supreme, all-pervading place—there, by force of the [oral] transmission, one's own form is contemplated into being.
**CMP 8.13**
Oh, how marvelous! Oh, the peaceful, the supra-sensory! Oh, the supremely profound buddhahood, the highest state! Thus [it is said].
**CMP 8.14**
Oh the Vajra! Oh the Vajra! Oh the teaching of the Vajra! Where there is no body, speech, or mind, there [the divine] form is contemplated into being. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 8.15**
It is also said by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka-pāda: "There is no hollowness in your body, nor flesh, bone, or blood; you have shown forth a body like a rainbow in the sky."
**CMP 8.16**
There is no disease, no impurity in [your] body, and no arising of hunger or thirst; [yet] by you, for the sake of conforming to the world, worldly activity has been displayed. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 8.17**
In the Sarvakalpasamuccaya too he says:
**CMP 8.18**
Having grasped the pure heart [-essence], [there is] the contemplation of the vajra-body; firm, substantial, without hollowness—he has attained the vajra-body. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 8.19**
(In Apabhraṃśa-flavored verse, addressing the goddess Prajñā:) "O you equal to space, free of dust, bearing the best of forms, bodiless, markless, daughter of wisdom; deep ocean of virtues, compassionate, peerless one—place your hand upon my head!" Thus [it is said].

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 8.colophon**
[Here ends] the eighth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa (apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa (non-abiding nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva's non-localized liberation)). // 8 //
**CMP 9.1**
Sealing the cause by the fruit and sealing the fruit by the cause—[that] is to be contemplated; for one who [seeks] accomplishment otherwise, it does not arise in a billion eons. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.2**
Vajrasattva, the great King, is to be invoked again and again. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.3**
Having given up idle lounging (lit. "stretching out the feet") and abandoned the basket [-load] of saṃsāra, one should accomplish the foremost Vajrasattva, the mind ever exerted.
**CMP 9.4**
Having earnestly abandoned regret, sloth-and-torpor, and the rest—otherwise there would be no attainment, not even in a hundred billion eons. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.5**
Those who are fixed here in the [mere] state of a monk, and the people who delight in [dry] reasoning, and those fixed in the state of [proud] elders—to them one should not teach the reality. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.6**
Knowledge devoid of [tantric] means, and the [moral] training too, was taught for the disciples (śrāvakas), O great Hero; lay hold of [the deeper meaning] in their case [as well].
**CMP 9.7**
In the root tantra (mūlasūtra (the root tantra cited as authority)) too he says: "Those devoid of [this] knowledge desire [merely] the ten paths of wholesome action." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.8**
(In MIA-flavored verse:) "You have trained in the vehicle of the disciples, O monk; [yet] one should course there in the bodhisattva-conduct. Course in the conduct of awakening among the qualities of a Buddha—this is to become the [very] ground of the Self-Existent One." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.9**
By harsh, severe ascetic observances the body, afflicted, withers away; from suffering the mind is distracted, and from distraction the attainment [turns out] otherwise [than intended]. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.10**
In the root tantra too he says: "When practiced by harsh, severe ascetic observances, he is not accomplished; but when [reality] is served (and the consort enjoyed) through the enjoyment of all the sense-pleasures, he is swiftly accomplished." Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.11**
Passion, aversion, and delusion—these three are [like] adhering poison; they become [deadly] poison [only] when served with [further] poison [i.e. unwisely].
**CMP 9.12**
But again they become the nectar of immortality when served with the nectar [of wisdom]. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.13**
That by which the dull-witted is bound—by that very thing the wise one is wholly released; through the contemplation of awakening, all this is reversed.
**CMP 9.14**
That by which the deluded are bound and are crushed in the [hell] Raurava—by those very [things] they are released, with ease, through the power of wisdom. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.15**
Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the supreme, all-encompassing [maṇḍala]: the Saṃvara of the Net of Ḍākinīs of the Union of All Buddhas (Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījāla-saṃvara).
**CMP 9.16**
In the supreme, delightful secret [abode], ever abiding as the all-self, the glorious one consisting of all Buddhas, the blissful arising of Vajrasattva [dwells].
**CMP 9.17**
Adorned with the great divine jewel-nets of the Tathāgatas and the rest; thereupon, in [a palace] ablaze with an outspread canopy hung with bells—

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 9.18**
—performing vajra-song and worship with songs and instrumental music, by means of flowers, incense, and the rest, and likewise with lamps, perfumes, and so on—
**CMP 9.19**
—they accomplish, in a dwelling or again in [a place] with a garden and the like, the Saṃvara of the Net of Ḍākinīs of the Union of All Buddhas.
**CMP 9.20**
There, first installing a seat, comfortable and soft to the touch, covered with the cloth of the universal lotus—that is the all-pure seat.
**CMP 9.21**
[There is] the Union of All Buddhas, the magical display of the Lord of Yoga; for there indeed [the deities] in the forms of glorious Vajrasattva manifest [themselves].
**CMP 9.22**
Consisting of all the elements, and likewise consisting of the root of life—by [the consorts] facing one's own tutelary deities, [there is] the setting-in-motion of the seal of attainment.
**CMP 9.23**
One should imagine the emblem-seal—cast, or fashioned, or [otherwise] wrought, finely painted, and bearing varied reflected images.
**CMP 9.24**
On those seats one should deposit all the [vital] breaths, each in its proper place; [the maṇḍala is] four-cornered, four-gated, adorned with four archways (toraṇas); and one should join vajra, jewel, lotus, and the rest with their gate-guardian.
**CMP 9.25**
With [consorts] facing one's own tutelary deities, with the women well prepared, lovely with their own seal-emblems—one should imagine the assembly-maṇḍala.
**CMP 9.26**
Four-cornered, four-gated, adorned with four archways, fitted with four [demarcating] threads, beautified with eight pillars—
**CMP 9.27**
—wrought with [pendant] necklaces and half-necklaces, ornamented with fillets, garlands, and festoons, resplendent with bells and banners, decorated with fly-whisks and the rest—
**CMP 9.28**
—and with crescent-moons and vajra[-tipped] corners at the junctions of the gate-turrets, adorned with varied cloths [bearing] bird-rows, gradations, finials, and the like.
**CMP 9.29**
With the enjoyments of all the goddesses, partaken of at will, through union with one's own tutelary deity, one should worship one's own self.
**CMP 9.30**
He is worshipped through the subsequent yoga, with the bliss of all union; and savoring [it] fully, he is accomplished through the supreme yoga.
**CMP 9.31**
By this, the one whose self is all the Buddhas would be accomplished, by the bliss of the elixir—[attaining] glorious Vajrasattva-[hood], [with] long life, youth, health, and true bliss.
**CMP 9.32**
[He becomes] the great body of all Buddhas, the eloquence (Sarasvatī) of all Buddhas, the great mind of all Buddhas, the great festal radiance of all Buddhas;
**CMP 9.33**
the great King of all Buddhas, sovereign of all Vajra-holders, lord of all the Lords of the World, supreme master of all the Jewel-lords.
**CMP 9.34**
Taking his delight with those [goddesses], he attains arising [as a deity] for the one [thus] proceeding; as the great Adept of all the goddesses, he is accomplished as a Universal Monarch (cakravartin). Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.35**
Daily, or monthly, or yearly likewise, or else according to [his] resolve, he should enact the Saṃvara of the Buddhas [as a dramatic play]. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 9.36**
Whether standing or seated or pacing about or however positioned, whether rejoicing or talking, here or there, in whatever manner—
**CMP 9.37**
—whatever takes on the character of a sense-path, that, by its very nature, even through an uncomposed [non-formal] yoga, he should bear as consisting of all the Buddhas.

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 9.38**
Equal to space, space-like in form, comparable to the boundless ocean—[here] the method of the dharma of passion, [and even] aversion, [become] sport, an expanse of play.
**CMP 9.39**
Only the [bare] essential matter has been taken up, for the sake of instructing disciples; for how many further lifetimes could the teaching on passion be endured [if told in full]?
**CMP 9.colophon**
[Here ends] the ninth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages], concerning the manifoldness of the bodhisattva's conduct and the arising and full awakening of dharma, by the method of the glorious Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījāla-saṃvara. // 9 //
**CMP 10.1**
In the regions of the great forest, on a deserted mountain adorned with fruits, flowers, and the rest, this collection of meditations (dhyānasamuccaya (the compendium of meditative absorptions)) is to be accomplished.
**CMP 10.2**
Always enjoying the five strands of sense-pleasure—for those who, desiring knowledge, are [thus] impassioned. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 10.3**
The cultivation of the body, speech, and mind of the vajras of body, speech, and mind—that task [is to be done] by way of [their own] true nature; swift attainment is reached.
**CMP 10.4**
One should have made, according to the rite, a great image bearing a crown of matted locks, resembling white in color, wholly enclosed in the saṃvara of mantra.
**CMP 10.5**
Having taken a sixteen-year-old [consort], adorned with all ornaments, lovely of face and wide-eyed—having obtained [her], one should practice the consort-observance (vidyāvrata (the observance undertaken with a consort (vidyā))).
**CMP 10.6**
By the enjoyments of the rank of Locanā, with the vajra-emblems, one should cultivate [the union]—[with her who is] versed in the procedure of seal and mantra, well trained in mantra and tantra,
**CMP 10.7**
—he should make [her] a Tathāgata-consort, established in the awakening of a Buddha; the holder of the great observance should perform the secret worship at the four junctures [of day / with the four beings].
**CMP 10.8**
He should undertake all food and nourishment with bulbs, roots, and fruits; thus one would swiftly become a Buddha, a lord [who is] an ocean of great knowledge.
**CMP 10.9**
He would attain all that in just six months—there is no doubt here; the practitioner of firm resolve should always wander in the forest for alms.
**CMP 10.10**
Frightened by fear, they give [him] food, divinely adorned; if they transgress, the vajra-self would [bring] the destruction [whose seed-]syllable is vajra.
**CMP 10.11**
Having obtained a goddess, a nāga-woman, a great yakṣiṇī, an asura-woman, or even a human woman, the consort-observance is to be practiced, served by the knowledge of the three vajras. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 10.12**
By the attainment [of union] of the two organs, [there is] the procedure of exertion within; the joyous mind of the sage, in [the moment of] accomplishment, is remembered as the great bliss (mahāsukha (great bliss, the supreme tantric realization)).
**CMP 10.colophon**
[Here ends] the tenth chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] conduct free of conceptual elaboration (niṣprapañca (free of conceptual elaboration)). // 10 //
**CMP 11.1**
On secluded mountains, and by rivers and springs, and in cremation-grounds and the like, this collection of meditations is to be practiced.
**CMP 11.2**
And the knower of reality should always, in truth, abandon the [ritual] practices and the rest; except for the "I-making" (ahaṃkāra) of Vajrasattva, he should make [no ego-clinging] elsewhere.

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
**CMP 11.3**
Even the [ritual] practices are not [needed to be] cognized when the pure reality is established—so long as that is being examined through union with the state of selflessness (nairātmya).
**CMP 11.4**
For one who abides in the state of non-inherent-nature and is endowed with divine means, whatever is prompted by intention is accomplished without [further] deliberation.
**CMP 11.5**
By the power of the yoga of cultivation, all that—whatever has the mark of attainment—presents itself of its own accord, in a single moment.
**CMP 11.6**
Should one regard the inner dharmas—form and the rest—it is called insight (vipaśyanā); should one imagine [them] as Akṣobhya and the rest, each in due number, it becomes calm-abiding (śamatha).
**CMP 11.7**
Because both of these are without inherent nature, [there is] that which is named the peace of suchness (tathatā); the yogin should make all the Buddhas enter into the maṇḍala of suchness. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 11.8**
In the great terror of the fire of nirvāṇa, not even an ash is released [unconsumed]; there reality is not found, nor the objects of the senses, nor the elements.
**CMP 11.9**
When the hero, free of conceptual construction, having forsaken the worldly mode of being, performs all [his] actions, then the Buddhas behold that.
**CMP 11.10**
He should move about like a child, [yet] with method, his doubts severed on every side; when the yogin is effortless, then the [spiritual] attainments rain down.
**CMP 11.11**
For those joined with every sin, well-fixed in the obscuration of delusion, through the yoga of the observance of the madman (unmatta-vrata), there come unfailing attainments within six months.
**CMP 11.12**
He would behold all the Buddhas himself; he is fulfilled with all desires; [there is] no waning and no diminishment—a body is born [for him] with life-span at his own will.
**CMP 11.13**
He fully attains the unsurpassed, supreme awakening without effort; without effort those eager for the bliss of all desires are accomplished.
**CMP 11.14**
Standing or seated, he should ever go to the profound state; through skill in the knowledge of the clear light (prabhāsvara (clear light, luminosity)), this is always the mark of the yogins.
**CMP 11.15**
By this yoga of meditation the jewel of the mind would become firm; and the Buddhas, established in awakening, grant [their] blessing-empowerment.
**CMP 11.16**
Having thus become settled, intent upon contemplation, the wise one, of concentrated mind, should cultivate [it] until the mind grows weary.
**CMP 11.17**
But when wearied, he should afterward wander about, acting as he pleases; with eyes slightly opened he should cultivate the vast awakening.
**CMP 11.18**
Laughing, talking, standing somewhere, somewhere he should set [his practice] in motion.
**CMP 11.19**
With mind attached to cultivation, [acting] in such a way that no weariness arises.
**CMP 11.20**
For the mantra-practitioner thus endowed with samādhi, free of conceptual construction, the unsurpassed state is attained, [all] limits of time abandoned. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 11.21**
[The signs of attainment are:] subtle form, light touch, pervasion and attainment-[at-will], radiance, steadiness, and mastery culminating in [the fulfillment of] every wish. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 11.22**
He sees [himself] as having attained the foremost knowledge of awakening, radiant as a Buddha; and he sees himself, lightly, as the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) of a Buddha.
**CMP 11.23**

title: Caryāmelāpakapradīpa
text:
He sees [himself] being worshipped by the great beings of the triple realm, and surely by Buddhas and bodhisattvas, with the five strands of sense-pleasure.
**CMP 11.24**
He constantly sees [himself] worshipped, the source of foremost great knowledge—[as] Vajrasattva, the great image, [as] Vajradharma of great renown.
**CMP 11.25**
He of great renown, [holder of] the secret vajra, sees his own image in a dream; the great Buddhas and the vajra-bearing bodhisattvas bow down [to him].
**CMP 11.26**
They will see such dreams, bestowing the attainment of body, speech, and mind—[and] a lovely goddess-maiden, complete with all ornaments.
**CMP 11.27**
Seeing a boy [and] a girl, he attains the accomplishment; he surely sees [himself] dwelling in the field of all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
**CMP 11.28**
With gladdened mind they give [him] the delightful treasury of Dharma—a body set upon the wheel of Dharma, surrounded by all beings.
**CMP 11.29**
He sees [this] at the time of yoga, established in the vajra of meditation. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 11.30**
Nothing is to be taken away from this, nor anything to be added; the real is to be seen as real—the one who sees the real is released. Thus [it is said].
**CMP 11.31**
And it is said in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra: "The Buddha does not [truly] pass into final nirvāṇa, nor does the Dharma perish; [yet] for the ripening of beings he displays [the appearance of] final nirvāṇa."
**CMP 11.32**
It is also said in the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra: "For nothing here arises through conditions, nor is [anything] ceased [by them]; it is only the [imagined] conditions that are constructed as arising and ceasing."
**CMP 11.33**
Therefore it is said: "With whatever state of being the minds of people are joined, by that they take on the nature of that—like a gem [that takes on] every color [reflected in it]."
**CMP 11.34**
That [process of] arising is conventional truth; death (the dissolution into clear light), indeed, is what is called ultimate truth. He who, through the guru's grace, becomes the knower of these two stages—he is a buddha-to-be.
**CMP 11.35**
The entry into the two truths [is] as if non-dual; though of unbroken form, it is indeed [a matter of] no [real] distinction. He by whom it is understood that "there is just unity of these two"—he is liberated.
**CMP 11.36**
Should someone fall from the summit of a great mountain, he might not wish to fall, yet he falls all the same; [so too] by the guru's grace, through the bestowed instruction, [the realizer] might not [even] wish for liberation, yet he is liberated all the same.
**CMP 11.37**
(The author's closing verse:) Reflecting on beings, and observing in the world the lack of capacity to attain reality—as if [gathering light] from a lamp-spark scattered by the breaking of the high waves of the ocean—approaching [the sources] little by little and gathering [them], this book has been composed by me; for those fortunate ones who are afraid of [taking] conventional truth [as ultimate], may it become a firebrand [to light their way].
**CMP 11.colophon**
[Here ends] the eleventh chapter, the resolution of doubts about the integration [of the stages, concerning] conduct utterly free of conceptual elaboration (atyanta-niṣprapañca (utterly free of conceptual elaboration)).
**CMP work-colophon**
[Work colophon:] This Caryāmelāpaka-pradīpa (Lamp that Integrates the Practices) is completed. // This is the work of the venerable great master Āryadeva.
